It is clear, connected, and convincing."},{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to a partner. Read your thesis aloud. Then name one change you plan to make today based on your peer feedback."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one change you plan to make to your essay today, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My partner said my second paragraph talks about Percy's loyalty but never says how it connects to my thesis about friendship. Students apply them to a model, then to their own writing.","activities":[{"id":"lab-clean-sentences","title":"Clear, Consistent, Concise","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.2.d","W.6.2.e","W.6.4"],"routine":"Mini-Lesson with Guided Practice","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Display the three sentences below. Students will see how each editing problem makes the writing harder to follow."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"1. Percy shows justice when he defends Grover. Later, the story says fairness is important, so Percy's sense of right is strong. 2. Annabeth is smart and clever and intelligent, and she plans carefully. 3. Percy and Grover walk toward Luke, and he looks nervous."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Writers do three final checks. First, terminology: choose one term for an idea and stick with it, unless you are deliberately comparing two ideas. In sentence one, justice and fairness appear to mean different things, so a reader gets confused. If I mean fairness, I should say fairness each time. Second, redundancy: in sentence two, smart, clever, and intelligent say the same thing. I keep one, intelligent, and cut the rest. Third, pronoun reference: in sentence three, who does he mean, Percy, Grover, or Luke? I replace he with the name."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How would you fix sentence three?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I would write 'Luke looks nervous' so the reader knows he means Luke, not Percy or Grover."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why does it matter to use the same term for a theme throughout an essay?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"If I switch between justice and fairness, the reader might think I am talking about two different ideas. Using one term keeps my thesis clear."},{"type":"directions","text":"Pick one body paragraph from your essay. Underline your theme terms and make them consistent. Cross out one redundant word or phrase. Circle every *he*, *she*, *it*, or *they* and make sure the reader knows who or what it refers to."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Watch for students who change every theme word. Explain that varied vocabulary is fine for ordinary words but a theme term in the thesis should stay consistent."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"These three checks will help you in the next part, where you will finish the whole essay."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students notice and revise unclear or repetitive language to build precise formal sentences and add detail with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Let's find the repeated words.' Model: 'Smart, clever, and intelligent mean the same thing. I will keep intelligent.' Provide frames: 'In my essay, I use the term ___ for the theme.' 'I replaced ___ with ___ so the reader knows who I mean.' 'I added ___ (when/how/where/why) to give more detail.' Example adverbials: 'at the end of the story,' 'bravely,' 'because he wanted to protect his friend.'","watchFor":"If students cannot find a redundant phrase, then read the paragraph aloud together and listen for repeated meanings. If students make every pronoun a noun, then explain that pronouns are fine when the reference is clear. Success: the student revises one sentence for consistent terminology, redundancy, or pronoun clarity and can explain the change using a frame."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding problems in their own writing","tryThis":"Give a three-item checklist (one theme term, no repeated meanings, clear pronouns). Have a partner read the paragraph aloud while the writer marks trouble spots."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students scan the whole essay for a theme word used inconsistently and write a note explaining which term best fits their thesis and why."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students finalize the essay by checking each paragraph against the thesis, verifying evidence and sources, and polishing formal style and format. Then they rehearse their key claim and evidence for the seminar or podcast.","activities":[{"id":"lia-finalize-essay","title":"Finalize the Explanatory Essay","minutes":20,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.b","W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","W.6.2.e","W.6.2.f","W.6.4","W.6.6","W.6.8","W.6.9","W.6.9.a","W.6.10"],"routine":"Independent Writing with Checklist","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"Passages cited in each student's essay"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let me model the thesis-connection check. My thesis says that Percy's loyalty to his friends shows the value of friendship across cultures. I read my second paragraph. It describes Percy going back for Grover, and it quotes the text. But the last sentence does not mention friendship. So I add: 'This choice shows that friendship, not personal safety, guides Percy's actions, just as loyalty was prized in ancient Greek stories.' Now the paragraph clearly supports my thesis."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What question can you ask at the end of each paragraph to check the connection to your thesis?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I can ask, 'Does this paragraph help prove my thesis? Did I say how?'"},{"type":"directions","text":"Use your revision checklist to finalize your essay. 1) Thesis: Read your thesis aloud. Is it clear and does it name the shared lesson or value? 2) Paragraphs: Check that each paragraph ends with a sentence explicitly tying evidence to the thesis. 3) Evidence: Make sure each paragraph has at least one quotation or paraphrase from *The Lightning Thief* or your second source, with the page or source named. Check that you paraphrased in your own words and did not copy. 4) Transitions: Add transition words (for example, *similarly*, *in contrast*, *as a result*) between ideas. 5) Style: Remove slang and contractions. Use precise words. 6) Conclusion: Make sure the ending follows from your explanation and does not add a brand new idea. 7) Format: Add a title and, if it helps the reader, a heading. Keyboard or neatly copy the final version, and include your source list."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Confer with two or three students whose peer feedback showed the biggest gaps. Ask them to point to the sentence they will fix first. Students using computers should save their work and may type their final copy; students writing by hand should copy neatly."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Check source credibility and attribution. If a student relies on a source of questionable quality, ask: 'Who wrote this, and how do they know?' Redirect to a stronger source if time allows."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["W.6.2","W.6.9"],"stem":"A student's paragraph quotes Percy going back for Grover, but the paragraph's final sentence does not mention the thesis about friendship. What should the student do?","choices":[{"text":"Add a sentence that explains how the evidence shows friendship guiding Percy's choice.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. A final sentence that links evidence to the thesis makes the paragraph's purpose clear to the reader."},{"text":"Add another quotation about a different character.","correct":false,"rationale":"More evidence without explanation does not connect the paragraph to the thesis; the problem is a missing link, not a lack of quotations."},{"type":"x","text":"Delete the quotation because quotations are not needed in an essay.","correct":false,"rationale":"Quotations are a key way to support a thesis. Removing it would weaken the paragraph."},{"text":"Change the thesis so it no longer mentions friendship.","correct":false,"rationale":"The paragraph should be revised to support the thesis, not the other way around, unless the whole essay's focus has changed."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students revise and finalize writing with attention to detail, cohesion, and formal register, using adverbials to add precision.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Read your thesis. Then read one paragraph. Does the paragraph prove the thesis?' Provide frames: 'This evidence shows that ___ because ___.' 'As a result, ___.' 'In contrast, ___.' 'In the story, Percy acts ___ (how) when ___ (when).' Encourage students to expand one sentence with an adverbial of time, manner, place, or cause, such as 'during the quest,' 'bravely,' 'on the bus,' or 'because he trusts his friend.'","watchFor":"If students write only simple short sentences, then model adding one 'when' or 'why' phrase. If students copy phrases from the text without quotation marks, then remind them to quote or paraphrase. Success: the student writes at least one sentence that links evidence to the thesis and includes an adverbial that adds detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finishing the full essay in time","tryThis":"Have students prioritize: thesis, one strong body paragraph with thesis connection, and a conclusion. Offer sentence starters and allow a partner to read aloud while the writer revises."},{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting evidence to the thesis","tryThis":"Give the frame 'This evidence shows ___, which supports my thesis that ___.' Have the student underline the thesis words in the paragraph."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students add a sentence that compares the value in *The Lightning Thief* with a value in a second text, and check that the comparison supports the thesis."}]}]},{"id":"lia-seminar-prep","title":"Prepare Key Claims for the Seminar or Podcast","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.9","W.6.9.a","W.6.10"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Tomorrow you will talk about your ideas, not just read your essay. Choose your one strongest claim and your best piece of evidence so you can say them clearly. Your format may be a seminar or a podcast, so think about how your voice and your evidence work together to teach your listeners."},{"type":"directions","text":"On an index card or in your notebook, write: 1) My key claim, 2) My strongest evidence (a quotation or paraphrase with its source), and 3) One connection to a modern value (such as fairness, loyalty, or courage). Then practice with a partner. Partner A shares, and Partner B tells one thing that was clear and one question they still have. Switch."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is your key claim, and what evidence best proves it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My claim is that Percy shows loyalty by risking himself for Grover. My best evidence is when Percy refuses to leave Grover behind even though it is dangerous. That connects to a modern value because people today still admire friends who stand by each other."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How can a listener tell your evidence supports your claim?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I can say 'This shows' or 'This proves' after my evidence and explain the link in one sentence."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Choosing an appropriate format (written essay now, spoken seminar or podcast tomorrow) is part of the task. Remind students that the same claim and evidence can be communicated differently: more concise and conversational aloud, but still accurate."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students rehearse oral explanation of a claim and evidence, using clear academic phrases and adverbials to add detail.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Tell your partner your claim first, then your evidence.' Provide frames: 'My claim is that ___.' 'The strongest evidence is ___ (source).' 'This shows ___ because ___.' 'This connects to today because ___.' Encourage students to use adverbials such as 'in the story,' 'bravely,' or 'because he cares.' Allow rehearsal in a home language before shifting to English.","watchFor":"If students can only read their essay aloud, then prompt: 'Say it in your own words in one sentence.' If students name evidence without a claim, then prompt: 'What does this evidence prove?' Success: the student states a claim, names evidence, and links the two aloud."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: speaking without reading","tryThis":"Have the student record the claim, evidence, and connection in three bullet notes and practice with a partner using only the notes."},{"type":"situation-placeholder","situation":"","tryThis":""},{"type":"support-table","rows":[]}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how their essay has grown and identify any final steps before tomorrow.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Final Check Quick Write","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.4","W.6.10"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write your response to the question."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is the strongest improvement you made to your essay today, and what is one thing you still need to finish before tomorrow?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My strongest improvement was connecting each paragraph to my thesis about loyalty. I also made my theme word the same throughout. I still need to type my final copy and add my source list before tomorrow."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Optional sentence starter: *The best change I made was ___.
